Stage 3 · Grammar

Everything moves one step back

Somebody spoke. Now you are repeating it, later, somewhere else.

Read what he said, and what you would say afterwards.
  • “The best ad I’ve seen had a serious point.”
  • He said the best ad he’d seen had had a serious point.
Why does had become had had?
Direct speech reproduces a moment. Reported speech relocates it.

When you tell somebody what another person said, you are speaking from a different time and place than the original speaker was. Reported speech is how English adjusts for that. The verbs, the pronouns and the time and place references all shift to match your new position, and that shifting is not decoration — it is what marks the words as belonging to a past moment.

The core adjustment is the tense shift: each verb moves one step further back. Present becomes past, past becomes past perfect, will becomes would, can becomes could, must becomes had to. ‘It won’t make any difference,’ he said becomes He said it wouldn’t make any difference. Two things do not shift, because there is nowhere further back to go: the past perfect, and the modals would, could, should and might.

The shift is also not always obligatory. If what was said is still true, or if your reporting verb is in the present, you can leave the tense alone: She says the weather is the biggest problem is perfectly correct if it still is. Learners often apply the shift mechanically and produce sentences that sound oddly distanced from facts that have not changed.

Alongside the tenses, the pronouns and the time and place words must be adjusted to your point of view: I → she, my → her, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there. And one lexical point causes endless trouble: say takes no person, tell requires one. He said that… or He told me that… — never he said me and never he told that.

Before you look at the table: the table below shows each direct form with its reported equivalent. Work down the tense column first; the pronoun and time shifts are easier once the tense pattern is automatic.
The shift — one step back, every time
They saidYou report
present simple — “It is effective.”past simple — He said it was effective.
present continuous — “They are hoping…”past continuous — She said they were hoping…
past simple — “It had a serious point.”past perfect — He said it had had a serious point.
present perfect — “I ’ve seen…”past perfect — He said he had seen…
will — “It won’t make a difference.”would — He said it wouldn’t make a difference.
can — “No one can do it.”could — She said no one could do it.
past perfect · would · couldno change — they are already as far back as they go
Everything else that moves
TypeThey saidYou report
People“I saw your advert.”He said he had seen my advert.
Time“last winter” · “now” · “next year”the previous winter · then · the following year
Place“here” · “this”there · that
Reporting verbs said · told me · explained · mentioned · admitted · claimed · added

Tell needs a person; say does not take one. He told me it was funny or He said it was funny — never He said me.

That is optional. She said that it worked and She said it worked are both correct. In speech it usually disappears.

The shift is not always compulsory. If it is still true now, you can leave the present: He said the campaign is still running. Shifting it is never wrong, though, so shift when in doubt.

Choose the reporting verb deliberately. He claimed signals doubt. He admitted signals that it was awkward for him. He explained signals that it was reasonable. The verb carries your opinion, and readers notice.

Full grammar reference — reported speech

What it is

Reported or indirect speech is how you tell somebody what another person said, without quoting their exact words. Because the moment of speaking has moved, the verb tenses, the pronouns and the time and place references all shift to match the new point of view.

What it means, and what it does

Direct speech reproduces a moment; reported speech relocates it. ‘It won’t make any difference,’ he said puts you back at the moment he spoke. He said it wouldn’t make any difference tells the story from where you are now. The tense shift is not decoration — it is what marks the words as belonging to a past moment rather than to the present.

When and why we use it

When you tell somebody what another person said, you are speaking from a different time and place than the original speaker was. Reported speech is how English adjusts for that. The verbs, the pronouns and the time and place references all shift to match your new position, and that shifting is not decoration — it is what marks the words as belonging to a past moment.

The core adjustment is the tense shift: each verb moves one step further back. Present becomes past, past becomes past perfect, will becomes would, can becomes could, must becomes had to. ‘It won’t make any difference,’ he said becomes He said it wouldn’t make any difference. Two things do not shift, because there is nowhere further back to go: the past perfect, and the modals would, could, should and might.

The shift is also not always obligatory. If what was said is still true, or if your reporting verb is in the present, you can leave the tense alone: She says the weather is the biggest problem is perfectly correct if it still is. Learners often apply the shift mechanically and produce sentences that sound oddly distanced from facts that have not changed.

Alongside the tenses, the pronouns and the time and place words must be adjusted to your point of view: I → she, my → her, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there. And one lexical point causes endless trouble: say takes no person, tell requires one. He said that… or He told me that… — never he said me and never he told that.

Typical situations

You need reported speech for passing on messages, telling somebody what was decided in a meeting, quoting research or the news, and recounting any conversation you were part of.

  • Reporting a statement — the core use, with say or tell.He said (that) it was just one light.
  • Reporting an opinion — think, believe, feel in the reporting verb slot.She said the weather was one of the biggest problems homeless people had.
  • Reporting a plan — the future shifts back too.She mentioned they were hoping more countries would do it next year.
  • Reporting an admission or a claim — the reporting verb carries the attitude.He admitted he had made a mistake. · She claimed she hadn’t seen it.
  • Reporting an explanation — explain keeps to before the person.He explained that no one liked being told what not to do.
  • Reporting an instruction — tell + object + to + base verb.The instructor told them to use their phones while driving.
  • Reporting something still true — the shift is optional for permanent facts.She said the weather is / was the biggest problem.

How it differs from similar structures

say + (that) + clause · tell + somebody + (that) + clause. If a person follows the verb directly, it must be tell.
tell somebody that = report a statement · tell somebody to = report an instruction. He told me that it was late vs He told me to hurry.

How to build it

Statement: reporting verb (+ object) + (that) + clause with tenses one step back
say + (that) + clause  (no person)  ·  tell + somebody + (that) + clause
Instruction: tell / ask + somebody + to + base verb
Tense shift: present → past · past → past perfect · will → would · can → could · must → had to
Present simple → past simple‘It is one light.’ → He said it was one light.
Present continuous → past continuous‘They are hoping.’ → She said they were hoping.
Past simple → past perfect‘Many died.’ → She said many had died.
Present perfect → past perfect‘A law has been passed.’ → He said a law had been passed.
will → would‘It won’t matter.’ → He said it wouldn’t matter.
can / must → could / had to‘You must prove it.’ → He said they had to prove it.
Pronouns shift‘I saw your ad.’ → She said she had seen my ad.
Time and place shiftnow → then · today → that day · yesterday → the day before · tomorrow → the next day · here → there · this → that
No tense shift neededafter a present reporting verb: She says she is tired.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • Say and tell are not interchangeable. Say takes no person, or takes to: He said that…, He said to me that… Tell requires a person straight after it: He told me that… He said me and He told that are both wrong.
  • The tense shift is not obligatory when the reported statement is still true or the reporting verb is present: She said the weather is the biggest problem is perfectly correct if it still is.
  • The past perfect does not shift further — there is nowhere further back to go. ‘I had already left’ → He said he had already left.
  • Would, could, should, might and ought to do not change either: ‘I would go’ → She said she would go.
  • That can almost always be omitted in speech and informal writing: He said (that) it wouldn’t matter. Keep it in formal writing for clarity.
  • Choose the reporting verb for meaning: admit, claim, explain, mention, promise, warn, complain, insist, suggest all say something the neutral say does not. Suggest takes -ing or that, never somebody to do.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • He said me that it was just one light. → He told me that it was just one light. / He said that it was just one light.Say does not take a person directly.
  • She told that the weather was the problem. → She said that the weather was the problem.Tell needs a person after it.
  • He said that he will turn the light off. → He said that he would turn the light off.Will shifts to would after a past reporting verb.
  • She asked me what did I think. → She asked me what I thought.Reported clauses keep statement word order — see Lesson 35.
  • He explained me the idea. → He explained the idea to me.Explain requires to before the person.
  • The instructor told to them to use their phones. → The instructor told them to use their phones.Tell takes the object directly, with no to.

More examples in context

  • statementHe said it was just one light and it wouldn’t make any difference.
  • opinionShe said the weather was one of the biggest problems homeless people had.
  • planShe mentioned they were hoping more countries would do it the following year.
  • explanationHe explained that no one liked being told not to do something.
  • report of a ruleThe instructor told them that a new law had been passed.
  • instructionThe instructor told them to prove they could use a phone while driving.
  • admissionHe admitted he had never actually watched the whole advert.
  • claimThe company claimed the campaign had changed people’s behaviour.
  • still trueShe says the best adverts are the ones that make you laugh.
  • time shiftHe said he had seen it the day before.

A tip for remembering it

Report in three passes and nothing gets left behind. Pass 1: move every verb one step back. Pass 2: change the pronouns to match the new speaker. Pass 3: change the time and place words (today → that day, here → there). Then check the reporting verb: if a person comes straight after it, the verb must be tell, not say.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Reported speech shifts tenses one step back: present → past, past → past perfect, will → would.
  2. Pronouns and time and place references shift too.
  3. Say takes no person; tell requires one immediately after it.
  4. The past perfect and would, could, should, might do not shift further.
  5. No shift is needed if the statement is still true or the reporting verb is present.
  6. Choose the reporting verb for meaning: admit, claim, explain, promise, warn.
